note: A second fixture, asked for as a client stand-up: one Nestor for a fictional client's intake, one for reviewing this repo. Two desks, one package, two custom matchers — and the pairing is what found §6.40 and §6.41, because each desk alone hides the defect the other shows.

decisions.question: The client wanted two Nestors. Is that two demos, or one?
decisions.commitment: One file, demo/two_desks.py, holding both desks.
decisions.why: The finding only exists in the comparison. On the review desk alone the bug is invisible — its matcher implements the optional score(), so a rewritten key costs nothing and every seal serves. On the intake desk alone it reads as the operator's mistake in a matcher she wrote. Side by side, in one run, it is the package: identical bug, identical endpoint, and the only difference is a method the seam says is optional. Splitting them would file each half under the desk that has it, which is the framing that hid it.

decisions.question: Should the fixture seal through the library, where it works, or through nestor.ui, where it does not?
decisions.commitment: Through ui.dispatch, the same call the browser makes.
decisions.why: The whole claim is about what happens at the surface a human is allowed to use. A demo that reached past it to memory.add_pair(matcher=…) would be proving the opposite of the point — that the library is fine, which nobody doubted. Beat 4 does seal through the library once, to manufacture something reachable to then reject, and says so on screen rather than only in a reason field.

decisions.question: Is §6.40 one finding or two — the lost seal and the lost rejection?
decisions.commitment: One entry, two consequences, because it is one root cause and one fix.
decisions.why: Both are the UI writing through memory.get_matcher(None). Splitting them would invite two fixes for one defect, and the repo precedent is §6.37, which carried two consequences of one overwrite in a single entry. §6.41 is separate because it genuinely is a different question — not 'the UI re-keys' but 'an optional method decides whether that matters', which has three coherent answers and no obvious one.

decisions.question: Propose the fix?
decisions.commitment: No. Both entries land measured with the fix open, and the fixture queues the finding as a draft.
decisions.why: CLAUDE.md: anything touching persistence or the audit path gets an adversarial read before the PR. And the two candidate fixes are not equivalent — threading a matcher through ui.App is the one the mutation implements, but 'stop recomputing a key you are already holding' is smaller and fixes _seal_draft without settling what _seal or a fresh reject-match should do. Picking in the same change that found it is how the last three rounds each introduced a critical.

decisions.question: The eight gap assertions pass. Do they mean anything?
decisions.commitment: Proven by mutation, twice, before commit.
decisions.why: Implementing the ui.App.matcher fix turns all eight red and the run exits non-zero. Giving SerialMatcher the optional score(), touching nothing in nestor/, turns §6.41's red plus the two saying her seals are unreachable. Recorded because a gate nobody has watched fail is a description.

decisions.question: Did the first version of those assertions actually hold anything?
decisions.commitment: Not all of them. The beat-7 assertion was vacuous and was rewritten.
decisions.why: It compared the stored key to SerialMatcher.normalize(text) for a defect description containing no serial — where that matcher falls through to str(v).strip().lower(), which is byte-identical to StringMatcher's output for that string. It passed whether or not her matcher was installed. Rewritten around a description that quotes a serial, where all three matchers produce distinct keys. This is CLAUDE.md's 'a test that cannot fail', written by the session that had just read the rule, about an hour after reading it.

decisions.question: Two desks in one process share cascade's ledger path. Does the fixture care?
decisions.commitment: Yes — at_desk() switches it at every crossing, and a test reads both files.
decisions.why: The first draft set it once, so both desks wrote into the intake chain and beat 8 then reported the total as hers. That is a false claim in a fixture about audit trails. The switching is also honest about the same module-global problem beat 7 is about: scripts/two_instances.py does not have to care because it uses two processes.
